ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: The phrase occurs 150 times in 76 allowlisted texts.
EvidenceBody: In the records it regularly describes the impassability of the ancestral gate and places associated with Bodhidharma: "before Shaoshi Peak, not even water passes" (少室峰前，水泄不通) and "under the patriarch's gate, not even water passes" (祖師門下，水泄不通). One address sets it against "the Buddha-work gate, where wind passes and grass bends" (佛事門中，風行草偃). Another makes it one of three eyes: one is watertight and ordinary and initiated cannot be distinguished; one opens the whole earth and the ten directions are unobstructed; one surveys high and low and all kinds look up. The phrase also enters public questioning: "where not even water passes, is there still a way through?" (水泄不通處還有過也無). Thus an ordinary image of a perfect seal becomes a stock Chan description of a gate, peak, command, or point at which passage is challenged.
